workload.description: City scale: 24,000 driver location pings/s dwarfing 1,800 ride requests/s

assumptions.subject: workload
assumptions.statement: 30,000 operations/s for ONE city: ~96,000 online drivers pinging every 4 seconds = 24,000 pings/s, against only ~1,800 ride requests/s. The non-obvious result is that a ride-sharing system is a location-ingest system with a marketplace attached — the ping firehose, not the rides, is what sizes the fleet.

assumptions.subject: scope
assumptions.statement: This is a SINGLE-REGION, single-city deployment, which is the v1 scope of the engine. A real ride-sharing platform is sharded per city/region and the interesting failure modes are cross-region ones. Do not read this as a global architecture.

assumptions.subject: loc
assumptions.statement: Location ingest is deliberately a separate, cheap tier from the business API: a ping is a tiny write with no transaction, sized at ~8,000/s per instance. Putting pings through the same app tier as trip requests is the mistake this split exists to prevent.

assumptions.subject: q
assumptions.statement: Only ~25% of pings are persisted to the event log (visit_prob 0.25) — a driver stationary at a light produces no meaningful delta. Persisting every ping would nearly triple the log's write rate and its retention bill.

assumptions.subject: cache
assumptions.statement: The geo-index is Redis GEO (or S2/H3 cells) holding current driver positions: GEOADD on every ping, GEOSEARCH on every ride request. The engine charges both the same flat per-op rate; in reality a radius search over a dense city cell is far more expensive than a point write, and there is no spatial cost model here.

assumptions.subject: match
assumptions.statement: Dispatch is modelled as a per-request service at ~600 matches/s per instance, ~45 ms each. Real dispatch BATCHES requests over a 2-5 second window and solves an assignment problem across all waiting riders and drivers at once, because greedy per-request matching produces worse pairings. The engine has no batch-window or optimisation model, so this is the closest honest shape, not the real algorithm.

assumptions.subject: boundary
assumptions.statement: Maps, routing/ETA and the payment processor are OUTSIDE this model. Keystone has no per-instance price for a third-party API, so including one would mean inventing its cost. Their latency lands on the rider's experience and their rate limits can bind before anything modelled here does.

assumptions.subject: surge
assumptions.statement: Surge pricing, driver incentives, fraud checks and ETA prediction are not modelled. The one that matters for capacity is surge: it is a feedback loop that changes the arrival rate itself, and this is an open queueing network with a fixed offered load.

_library.summary: A driver-location firehose feeding a geo-index, with dispatch matching riders to nearby cars.
